utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, just for your information, yesterday when we spoke about the warning of the JNA of the 1st October 1991, Mr. Kostic said that he has seen a similar document, and this morning when he came into the courtroom he provided the B/C/S version to us. It will be copied and soon handed out to everyone. It's exactly the document that I referred to that Mr. Kostic identified in his collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, our thanks to Mr. Kostic and to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, yesterday we left talking about the Carrington Plan and the events of the 17th of October, 1991, and you had mentioned already during your testimony that you could not stay during the whole session of the Assembly session in Montenegro but that you had to go to Belgrade to attend a meeting in the SFRY Presidency. That's how it was; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And who attended the meeting in the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting of the Presidency was held in its reduced composition. Four members of the Presidency attended it: Mr. Borisav Jovic, Sejdo Bajramovic, Jugoslav Kostic, and myself of all the members of the Presidency. I think that perhaps someone from the federal organs was there, but I'm not sure. The four of us were there, though.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Milosevic take part in this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Was there another meeting on the Carrington Plan on that same day involving many more people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with Lord Carrington's plan, I know only that the Assembly of Montenegro had a session, and in the afternoon the Presidency of the SFRY, which I have just mentioned, which I myself attended. I don't know any other meetings in connection with Lord Carrington's plan held on at that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: With the help of the usher, I would like to provide to Mr. Kostic and also everyone else a section from a book that Ms. Smilja Avramovic wrote, and it's called "Post Heroic War of the West Against Yugoslavia." Mr. Kostic, do you know that book? Avramov. It's Avramov. Sorry. Smilja Avramov. Mr. Kostic, do you know this book of Ms. Avramov?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: If you look at --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know it, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at page 274, the second last paragraph, and I just quote a part of it. She speaks about the Carrington Plan and then says: "Military leadership headed by General Kadijevic and some individuals from expert teams as well as a group of independent intellectuals being concerned about the fate of the country and offering the help to President Milosevic were of the opinion that the Carrington document should be turned down." And the last sentence of that paragraph, it says: "Participating in the talks on the Carrington document were also President Karadzic and President Babic. President Milosevic's speech in The Hague the following day was the synthesis of the said opinions." Mr. Kostic, that seems to me to indicate that on the 17th there was quite a major meeting on the Carrington Plan with Mr. Milosevic, Kadijevic, and experts, as is named here, and intellectuals. Do you know about that meeting? Did you hear of it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything at all about that meeting. This is the first time I've heard of it. I have always been of the conviction that on the day when the Assembly of Montenegro discussed the Carrington Plan - and this was the 17th of October - the Assembly of Serbia discussed the same plan. However, later on I learned that Mr. Jovic denied this later and that the Serbia -- Serbian Assembly did not have a session on that date. I did not check this. I didn't go into it any further, but I don't know anything about this meeting you're mentioning, and I can say nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would like to tender this page of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, the witness did not recognise the document, disagreed with the content, and Avramov gave evidence earlier in the Defence case and it could have been dealt with by her cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do we know in fact whether it was dealt with in her cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It wasn't, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm not aware of this, Your Honour, but my assumption would be that the book was not translated at that time. I see Ms. Tromp is nodding. Obviously this book wasn't translated at that time. Perhaps, could it be marked for identification, and it may be that we can discuss it with another witness who may have participated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would say no, bring it in when it's the time to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we'll do, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We'll not mark it for identification. If you can have it admitted at another time, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would like to refer you now to a press statement by Lord Carrington of the 25th of October, 1991. It's not an exhibit yet, and I would like to be -- this to be handed out. Mr. Kostic, it's an English document because it's from Lord Carrington and relates to the meeting that was held on the 25th of October, 1991, and it says here on the first page: "Let me say that once that the continuing -- let me say at once that the continuing attacks by JNA on Dubrovnik and Vukovar are very worrying and threatening. These are not besieged garrisons to be relieved, nor Serbian communities to protect. "The leadership of the JNA is acting in a totally unjustified fashion, bear a heavy responsibility, and are accountable for what they are doing." And he continues: "I would have wished to have said this to him -" meaning Mr. Kadijevic, General Kadijevic - "him face-to-face. He has always said that he would accept and abide by any agreed political solution. But from his statements and actions this week, it is clear that he is siding with one of the parties. General Kadijevic's assertion that he derives his authority from those whose seizure of the Federal Presidency in Yugoslavia on 3 October has been condemned internationally (and who have declined to attend today's plenary), cannot be sustained." Do you know about this press statement, this public statement of Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And is he -- he's correct when he says that the JNA is attacking Dubrovnik and Vukovar, although there are no besieged garrisons and there are no Serbian communities to protect. Is he right there? That was what ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, 15 years later, I wouldn't be able to recall every word from Mr. Carrington's statement, but in principle he objected to the effect that there were no Serb communities there or besieged garrisons. However, we expressed our dissatisfaction with Mr. Carrington's assessment. We felt it was extremely one-sided. Mr. Carrington attempted to leave us as the reduced Presidency out of The Hague conference and only after we protested did he invite us to the conference on the 18th and the 25th. Also, on the 5th of November, Mr. Carrington started The Hague conference by stating that the Croatian leadership had not respected the cease-fire agreement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Professor, you have answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution would like to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 950.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I would like to put another document to you from the Carrington documentation that was provided by the European -- It's also not yet an exhibit. Can it be provided. It's a Declaration on the Situation in Yugoslavia from the 28th of October, 1991, and it relates to this session that took place on the 25th of October, 1991, and I just want to quote one paragraph. It's the third -- or, rather, two paragraphs; the third and fourth on that page. It says: "Notably, the principles of no unilateral change of borders, protection of human rights, and rights of ethnic and national groups constitute universal, objective standards, which leave no room for compromise. "The European Community and its member States are appalled at constant violations of these principles. In this context they refer to the Serbian position in the Conference, the coup d'etat of four members of the Federal Presidency and their announcement of a plan aimed at the establishment of a Greater Serbia. The statements and actions of JNA, which were condemned in the Declaration on Dubrovnik of 27 October 1991, should also be seen in this light." Mr. Kostic, do you know this -- do you know this Declaration?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall this Declaration, but I can only say that this was a time when the European Community was radically changing its standpoint and its views on resolving the Yugoslav crisis, taking up an extremely one-sided position, diverging from its previous standpoints that a peaceful solution should be found, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 951.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like now to leave, because we don't have much time, I want to leave this Carrington Plan and now turn to the Vance Plan. Mr. Kostic, in the examination-in-chief, you spoke about -- in detail about the Vance Plan, and we have discussed it here already. You discussed it with Mr. Milosevic when you addressed Exhibit D333, tab 64, which has the text of the Vance Plan, more or less. Mr. Jovic, when he spoke about the Vance Plan, he said that all the work involved with the drafting of the Vance Plan was directed by Mr. Milosevic on behalf of the Serb side. Is that also your recollection, that he was basically the one?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who worked with Mr. Cyrus Vance on behalf of the Serbian side. Probably those advocating the preservation of Yugoslavia. Is that what you mean by the Serbian side? I don't know who talked to Mr. Cyrus Vance. I only know that I did not have occasion to meet Mr. Cyrus Vance except at a meeting in Podgorica when he was talking to Mr. Bulatovic and Mr. Djukanovic. At that time, Mr. Cyrus Vance, although he was a representative of the United Nations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Babic and the entire Croatian Serb leadership in Knin, when they rejected or, rather, did not want to accept this plan, they got pressure to agree. They were pressured to agree to it, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether you can describe it as pressure, but in any case, we invested a great deal of effort to get them to accept this plan. We had a 40-hour meeting, then two six-hour meetings, and finally I went to Glina to a meeting of the Assembly of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, where it was ultimately accepted. Because in our assessment, Mr. Cyrus Vance's plan was a peaceful option, whereas what Mr. Babic was advocating was a war option.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would like to put to you what Mr. Jovic said in this context, and we are discussing whether the Croatian Serb leadership was pressured. Can you please be -- can this -- it's from Exhibit 596, tab 1. That is the 89(F) statement of Mr. Jovic. And at paragraph 114, he said: "... I spoke with Milan Babic and told him that the plan for the arrival of peacekeeping forces will be adapted with or without him." And in that same paragraph, the last sentence is: "I came to the conclusion that if Babic continued to resist, then he will be replaced." Mr. Kostic, as you took part in these discussions on the Vance Plan, are you aware that Mr. Jovic actually threatened Mr. Babic with replacement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard Mr. Jovic threatening Mr. Babic with replacement. Had we had any intention to replace Mr. Babic or arrest him, we could have done that very easily in Belgrade. We wouldn't have wasted so much time trying to keep all the people there and trying to get their agreement to the plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But Mr. Babic was replaced, was he not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then. Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, on what basis would he have been arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood that to be the Prosecutor's question as regards replacement or arrest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... said if you had wanted, at any time you could have had him arrested because he was in Belgrade. On what basis would you have arrested him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you, I don't know whether I can give a proper interpretation. I'm not a lawyer, I'm an economist, but I was in a very responsible government position. We were in a situation of imminent threat of war. We felt that part of the Republic of Serbian Krajina was still part of the still existing Yugoslavia. If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you not give me a simple answer to the question? Can you not just tell me the basis on which you would arrest him? I don't need the history of Yugoslavia to tell me that, surely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not talking about history, Mr. Bonomy. I'm talking about a dramatic situation in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you can't answer the question, we'll just move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kostic, on that same page that you have in front of you there's also paragraph 115 of the Rule 89(F) statement of Mr. Jovic, and he says here, and I quote from the middle of it: "After huge problems with Milan Babic, Milosevic completely lost his nerve and issued a public announcement stating that he was terminating all cooperation with the current Krajina leadership and that he would resume it once the Serbs in Krajina had elected a new leadership." Do you remember that, that he made such a strong statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why you keep asking me about Mr. Jovic's book. Why don't you ask me what I talked to Mr. Milosevic about. As regards Babic, I never discussed him with Mr. Milosevic. During my examination-in-chief, however, I did mention that there was an erroneous impression that Mr. Milosevic had undivided influence on the leadership of the Serbs in the Serbian Krajina. I also said that for this reason he asked me to attend the Assembly session in Glina, and I also said that at that time Mr. Milosevic sent an open letter to the leadership of the Serbian Krajina and Mr. Babic, which caused a great deal of surprise in the general public. That's what I can say about this. Mr. Jovic here is talking about his conversation with Mr. Milosevic, and I know nothing about it so I can't tell you anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I was asking you not about Mr. Jovic but about the public announcement of Mr. Milosevic that -- requesting that the leadership in Knin would -- should be replaced. That was my question. But I see you refer only to the letter. Let us now hear what you said on two occasions in that context. Can we please have in Sanction played the first clip.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's better.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters have a reference, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Could you have a copy passed to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They should have a copy. It's the clip Exhibit 352, tab 88. Your Honour, I forgot to mention that it is actually already an exhibit. It's 352, tab 88.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We don't have any translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are we supposed to have a translation?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. There are three excerpts in the exhibit and tab 88 so we were trying to find the portion referred to.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. The first what is played starts with "Vice-president of the Presidency, Branko Kostic, describes the course of the talks ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. We've found it now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Vice-president of the Presidency Branko Kostic described the course of the talks to detail accusing Milan Babic of walking out of the conference and taking the representatives of Serbian Krajina with him. Kostic told the press that Paspalj approached them on his own initiative and offered to sign it after he consulted municipality representatives, as he informed the Presidency members. Kostic then said that Babic's request to amend Vance's plan practically implied its refusal and that there was no justification for the request to return to political topics either, as Vance's plan did not prejudice a solution for the status of Krajinas. Kostic refuted the allegations about a possible coup in Krajina and explained that an order was being prepared on the organisation of life in the territories where the army was present. He explained that nobody made any physical threats at the conference, as Babic alleged, and that Blagoje Adzic had offered his apologies to those present for his nervous behaviour. Kostic said that it was now crucial to inform people in the Krajina correctly and show that Vance's plan did not imply betrayal of Krajinas. "If people in Krajina chose Mr. Babic's option, this will then mean the option of war. That is certain. It will then mean that the people of Krajina are neither willing ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I don't know. It's still continuing in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is no reception, no tape, sound.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it's playing here. It's playing here on the computer that Ms. Dicklich has, with tone and everything.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are not receiving any tone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the issue we are looking out for here?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We are looking, actually, in particular this part that's not coming. Actually, Mr. Kostic is repeating that same threat, more or less, that Mr. Milosevic, according to Mr. Jovic, made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Why don't you just put it to him?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me just read to you what actually is also on the video. It says here, Branko Kostic speaking: "If the people of Krajina choose Mr. Babic's option, this will then mean the option of war. That is certain. It will then mean that the people of Krajina are neither willing to share their fate with the rest of Yugoslavia nor to respect its organs. I am telling you this as my personal opinion. This practically amounts to refusal to participate in the work of federal organs or to respect their decisions and consequently those of the Presidency as the Supreme Command, just as Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Kucan did it. This practically means an act of secession of that territory. It is difficult for me to believe that might happen." Mr. Kostic, did you say that on that occasion? We have it on the tape, actually.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the original, that is what I said, and I would repeat the same thing given that situation today as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But as I see it, Mr. Kostic, what you are saying here is basically, "If you do not agree to the Vance Plan, then we cut off you. You have to fend for yourself." That's at least how I understand it. Would that be the correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where do you read that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Here. It says: "It will then mean that the people of Krajina are neither willing to share their fate with the rest of Yugoslavia nor to respect its organs." That's actually saying -- and particularly the next: "This practically amounts to a refusal to participate in the work of the federal organs or to respect their decisions and consequently those of the Presidency as the Supreme Command, just as Mr. Tudjman and Mr. Kucan did. This practically means an act of secession of that territory."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That seems to be looking at it from the opposite point of view; that they would be seceding by their conduct, rather than he would be cutting them off, but it's for you to put the questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, what did you mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Bonomy. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then I would like to right now the -- hear now the second Sanction video related to Glina. And for the interpreters, it is a section that starts with: "Mr. Kostic, how are you? Welcome to Glina."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for the reference. We've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want me to answer your first question, what I meant by it? You asked me what I meant by it earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, and I thought you had answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. We covered that issue already. We are on to Glina now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. You had answered that already, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Mr. Kostic, how are you, welcome to Glina. You are here to attend the Krajina Assembly conference. What do you expect from that meeting? "Quite a large number of us arrived to participate in the work of the Serbian Krajina Assembly after attending a fairly extensive discussion at the Yugoslav Presidency. In order to, on the one hand, repudiate all accusations that have been unfoundedly spread among these people that we are leaving those people in the lurch. Also, to tell the Assemblymen of the Serbian Krajina Assembly, as well as to all people, that that is a crude lie, that we have been and are remaining by the side of these people. In addition, to help inasmuch as we can for reason to prevail and that these people, as well as the assemblymen, realise that that which has been gained through war until now can be defended by peace in the best possible way from now on, with the assurances of the Security Council, a world organisation, and the engagement of the Blue Helmets. "Thank very much on behalf of Novi Sad television. "Thank you. "Mr. Kostic, what is your message to the people of Glina and Krajina? "That we have stood by and are going to stand by these people. However, choosing between the peace option and the war option, the time has come to defend in peace what these people have gained by war. Not by a continuation of a long and precarious war that might spread out to the hinterland and Bosnia and sweep over entire Yugoslavia, or even wider, the Balkans. That could obviously finally result in the loss of everything these people gained by war so far."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just one question to this. At that time when you made this -- this speech, at that time, the Serb territories in Croatia, they were under control of the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time when I made that statement and when I was in Glina myself, the Serbs in those areas who were involved and engaged and stood up to all attempts on the part of the Croatian paramilitary to impose their own power upon them, they were in control of the territory. They had their freedom. They had their alphabet. They had everything which they had as a constituent people and pursuant to the Croatian constitution that was guaranteed to them on the basis of the constitution previously. So that's why I said that as they succeeded in defending themselves we should defend by means of peace and not by means of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic. Mr. Kostic, among the defence exhibits that Mr. Milosevic proposed to you was Defence Exhibit D333, tab 2, and I would like to -- you to turn to it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's an exhibit that was not yet tendered by Mr. Milosevic, and I would like to address it with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is a meeting with representatives that the Presidency held with representatives from the Serbian Krajina, held on the 3rd of January, 1992. Do you recall that meeting?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall it extremely well.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like you now first to turn to page 11 in the English where Mr. Milan Martic is addressing you, and he says the following, it's about disarming -- it's the talks about disarming the forces in Krajina, and Mr. Martic says the following: "The solution to this problem is simple, but what worries me most are, as we said, our local people who are fighting and the local army; there is no other army except for commanding officers. The weapons are a burning issue - the heavy weapons." And this is what you talk about. And in relation to this, on that same page, you say the following: "We said that all Territorial Defence is also part --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, but in the Serbian language, I haven't managed to find that section, what you're just reading out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 2. They are the stenographic notes from the meeting of the -- between members of the SFRY Presidency and representatives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's on page 16 in the -- in the B/C/S version, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I was reading from the lower part of that, and you say: "... we said that all Territorial Defence is also part of the JNA, but the disarming of the Territorial Defence has been planned. I am asking you: Do the UN and the group that will carry out control on the basis of the talks they had with you, have a summary and list of equipment - how many of these tanks, mortars, howitzers, artillery, and so on belongs to the Territorial Defence and how many to the Knin Corps. Do they have it?" And you give the answer "No." And then you continue: "Therefore, we will create conditions - you will not have to transport things from Banija down to Knin - we will deposit the equipment where it may be used in need. You practically have an already formed unit, which is convenient when so many men are from this area. You had units even before you publicly declared them organised. So, you will continue to have them organised. You can increase police units. You have the Army in the background if they need to intervene." Mr. Kostic, that is actually circumventing the Vance Plan, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. That's not correct, because the Vance Plan provided for the fact that on the territory where the Blue Helmets would be deployed in the operative political sense, nothing be changed, that everything should remain the same, including the organs of power and authority, the Territorial Defence, and everything else. But what it did provide for was that the weapons of the Territorial Defence, both light and heavy weapons, must be stored under a double key, and only when the Blue Helmets take up their positions in the territory and take on the physical protection of the Serb people there, only then would the Yugoslav People's Army withdraw, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when you say that -- when you stress here that the UN wouldn't have lists of materials, that's actually -- is that not basically saying, "We can cheat them"? "They wouldn't know how many material belongs to the TO and what to the JNA"? Or why do you say that here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the United Nations did not have a list of equipment and weaponry for the simple reason that they didn't ask for it. As far as the United Nations were concerned, the most important thing was that light and heavy weaponry should be deposited in certain storehouses, that it be under lock and key and under control, among other things, of the United Nations, so that when the Blue Helmets appear, the Yugoslav People's Army would withdraw completely from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. The question was whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The question was whether, when you say that the UN would not have a list of materials, whether you were not in effect saying that "We can cheat them."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not what I meant. Cheat them how? How would we cheat them?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you referred to the fact that the UN wouldn't know which material, heavy equipment, would belong to the TO and which belongs to the JNA, meaning you could leave the JNA stuff behind, claiming it were TO stuff. That's what actually is meant here, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Short answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply thought that the United Nations were absolutely not interested in what belonged to whom, that the United Nations were interested in the weaponry being deposited, that it be placed under their control, and that the JNA be withdrawn from that territory, and that's what was done.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, continuing in the text we have further questions. It probably should be two pages further on. And Milan Martic, actually, asked you: "If we must be wise with all this --" and it's on page 13 in the English, Your Honours. And page 19 in the Serbian language, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Martic says: "If we must be wise with all this, you ought to help us. You know that there are 50.000 soldiers in Krajina now. You print money here and send it to them. They are used to that money and they live somehow. The economy is not functioning, money is being printed." And your answer to this is: "They must understand that we print money here not only for them but also for these whom we send from here. This money printing cannot last indefinitely. This must be kept in mind." Mr. Kostic, was this how the Serb soldiers from the Krajina were financed, through money printing in Belgrade? Was that how it went?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please, take into account the fact that we're talking about Yugoslavia still, and there still were no internationally recognised republics. It was a united territory, the territory of Yugoslavia, and on that territory we had the strongest corpus or, rather, corps. It was the Knin Corps. And we had people there from all parts of Yugoslavia making up that Knin Corps, both the soldiers and the others. And the people lived there and they lived on money, and the Yugoslav People's Army financed that. So those are the people we're talking about here. I don't know which other people you mean. Who else would we send? Well, the Yugoslav People's Army was there. The man from Macedonia was there. The Split soldier who lost his life was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the TO members from Krajina, were they paid by the money being printed in Belgrade, before -- during this conflict and also after the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't give you a precise answer to that question, whether all the members of the Territorial Defence did, or were, but in view of the fact that we were dealing with wartime conditions, the Territorial Defence units shared the fate of the units of the Yugoslav People's Army. They come under the same command and so on and so forth, so it would be realistic to suppose that they were financed too. So that's why I say that we cannot keep it up that long, that the people who were engaged at the front should come back home and carry on making a living and living off that. So I can't give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to continue now, go a little bit further in the text. We are now -- in the English it's page 21, and in the Serbian -- it's an exchange with Mile Paspalj.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I find Mile Paspalj in the Serbian version on page 28, the middle of page 28. That's where he appears, Mile Paspalj. But I can tell you something --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually a little bit further, I think. It's where Mile Paspalj says: "First the period of three, four, or five months of pushing permanent conflict between prominent Krajina figures in the territory of Krajina, this did not come from the Republic of Croatia or Bosnia but precisely from the Republic of Serbia and Yugoslavia." And you answer to this: "I would appreciate it, Mr. Paspalj, if you discussed the issues concerning Serbia with the leadership of Serbia." It's on page 31, actually, in the Serbian language. Do you know what Mr. Paspalj is referring here to when he says "Serbia pushing permanent conflict between prominent Krajina figures"? Do you know what he means?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he said that, I said, and during the examination-in-chief I also said, that one of the reasons for the tragedy that the Serb people in the Republic of Serb Krajina suffered was on a political and ideological basis, that that was the grounds for that, and that Babic joined the Chetnik emigration and Bujic [phoen], and that the divisions in Serbia were highly present, both among the leadership and among the people, and that in all the contacts I had I insisted upon leaving behind ideology and politics but that they should see to their survival in the area first. And I know that certain opposition parties sent people there, their volunteers. And some people thought that they would start out from there towards Belgrade, under arms and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would like now to go a bit further. It's on page 23 of the English, and it's -- in the B/C/S, it's where you refer to the forces in the Krajina. And you say the following: "We are now, with this engagement of the peacekeeping forces, ensuring that you continue to have your own police and authorities in that territory, and for the 93 per cent men who are now on the front to take off their uniforms and return to work for a living, leaving all the weapons here and not grouping it in one place." And if you're looking, Mr. Kostic, it's page 55 in the Serbian. And you say: "I said, if need be, we will make new hangars and we will deposit these weapons there where they will be most accessible for use; 93 per cent of the troops remain here where they can be mobilised and engaged at any moment, and use those weapons. You can triple your police forces and you have mechanised units at the border of Krajina and Bosnia, which can reach the other end of the border within two hours." Mr. Kostic, that's another move against the Vance Plan, the demilitarisation, is it not, tripling the police? That was not what the Vance Plan foresaw; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But let me tell you this: First of all, the storing of weapons was agreed upon with Mr. Vance, that is to say Marek Goulding, who came here as an envoy of Mr. Cyrus Vance, and we specifically agreed about that, both the leadership of the Serbian Krajina with Marek Goulding, and we in the Presidency of the SFRY. That's one thing. Second thing is to -- the increase in the member -- numbers of the police was not something they were averse to because they felt that the Croatian authorities could infiltrate sabotage units and then blame the Serb people of having risen up against the Blue Helmets and things like that. So the peace forces, the UN peace forces, were also interested in having more policemen there to provide better security for themselves and the population as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: On the next page there in that same section, the next page in the English, page 24, you say the following: "Why were we in the situation where we had to accept many of these truces? Because we had enormous problems with the supply of manpower and replenishing the army. You must understand how much defeatism, rejection, and disorientation there is; to date 80.000 men have deserted or left the front. Also, the units that have been formed instead of setting out for the front simply disband and go home." And just my question to this, that you accepted the Vance Plan was basically a military necessity, was it not? You couldn't continue to fight. You didn't have the resources. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not a good conclusion on your part. We could have mobilised had we declared a state of war. We could have mobilised a million people, whereas the top military echelons only asked for 150.000, this additional mobilisation. However, had we not gone before the Security Council and brought in the Blue Helmets in Serbian Krajina, we would ultimately have had to declare a state of war, and we did not declare a state of war. The situation that you're talking about and these quotes from you, that is a situation where there was no state of war proclaimed, and when the army, to all intents and purposes, was working according to peacetime laws and not wartime laws. It was a very difficult situation because of which the army complained to us a great deal systematically and persistently.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, it's not my quote, it's your quote. I'm quoting you about what you said at that meeting with the Croatian Serbs. A paragraph below that you say the following --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You drew the wrong conclusion out of this. You drew the erroneous conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say the following, and it's on the same page, just the next paragraph: "I'm very sure that Serbia and Montenegro could have easily proclaimed themselves a state union, a sovereign state, and so on. But the moment this was done and accepted, every Yugoslav People's Army soldier would be an occupying soldier on the territory of Herzegovina, the Knin Krajina, and Western and Eastern Slavonia." And a little bit further down, you say: "This is why we promote the continuity of Yugoslavia, because of the international community, the legitimacy of the Yugoslav People's Army, and possibly to engage this force on the whole territory." That was the motivation; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, had we promulgated a state of Serbia and Montenegro, we would have gone against the valid constitution of Yugoslavia, and we were attempting to preserve this constitution and comply with it until the 27th of April, 1992. In other words, we didn't want to behave in the same way as the secessionist republics which rejected the Yugoslav constitution and declared independence. We were acting in accordance with the then valid constitution. It was the constitution of the only legitimate state that existed at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, this may sound as though I'm going back to earlier questions, but it's in this context I want to ask you this. When you assessed that there was an imminent state of war in October, who was that war between?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time we declared an imminent threat of war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, imminent threat of war, yes. Yes. Who was the imminent threat of war between?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When an imminent threat of war was declared, the war was between armed paramilitary formations of Croatia and the JNA, which is the armed forces of the SFRY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paramilitary of Croatia had armed men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was for the avoidance of doubt that I asked the question. That's a sufficient answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, a bit further down now in the text -- in the English, Your Honours, it's page 39; and in the B/C/S, it's 56. And it's actually an exchange between you and Mr. Risto Matkovic, and you say here: "We don't know where we will be tomorrow, but we should start from this: Whether there is a Yugoslavia or a Serbia in this shape or another, it is more than certain in my assessment that there is no government in Serbia that can survive and be prepared to sacrifice these people. It does not exist." And a little bit further down in relation to Montenegro, you also say: "However, the situation in Montenegro is such that there is no authority that would survive for 24 hours if they were prepared to betray the interest of those people." Mr. Kostic, that is actually what you are saying here. That's what I put to you when we spoke about Mr. Jovic's book, that the Serbian leadership and the Montenegrin leadership could not survive without supporting the Krajina Serbs. That's how I understood that -- your remark here. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not about the need for those in authority to survive in power. It's about the fact that the people of Serbia and Montenegro were convinced that physical protection had to be provided to other parts of the people that were under threat in other parts of Yugoslavia until a solution was found. The issue was not bare survival.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it says here no government in Serbia can survive. It's about power.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, it was the government that was democratically elected by the people in Serbia. And you should also mention Montenegro. At democratic multi-party elections, the people elected the government, both in Serbia and Montenegro. It was given the support of two-thirds of the people, and this support was owing to the programme, the platform. A large part of this was to try to preserve Yugoslavia, to try to find a peaceful solution, and to prevent the part of the people that was under threat in any part of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to move on now, and we go to the English page 52, and in the Serbian it's page 74. It's an exchange between you and Mr. Martic, Milan Martic, about, I would say, concrete terms. "I agree with what President Babic said, that we would observe the Presidency decision and that we ought to agree on concrete issues. Their troops on our territory - about 50.000 for whom money is being printed. According to our plan, we should transfer 20.000 men to the police. Are you prepared to provide for these 20.000 men; are you prepared for Adzic and Kadijevic not to order them to pull out the tanks, because we won't give them; nobody needs to convince us of that." And your answer is: "These are all concrete issues; it is cheaper to both Serbia and Montenegro to do this than to finance a war." And Martic: "Are you prepared to leave me a number of officers that we are requesting, who want to lead these units as police units. We need to specify all these details and stand behind it. This is what I am interested in." And your answer is: "I completely agree, these are the issues about which we have to sit down and talk. Those who are responsible for the portfolios should talk with the relevant portfolio minister, and this ought to have an appropriate form instead of us having reservations again each other." Mr. Kostic, these concrete arrangements for the payment of these 20.000 police people and what else Mr. Martic needed, these arrangements were made, were they not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that. The possibility is left open for an agreement of this. I really cannot tell you what was implemented and to what extent, referring to what was discussed here. It wasn't only about 20.000 policemen. It was also about how various services could function, such as the post office, the telephone communications, the public auditing service, and so on and so forth. The -- bringing in the peace forces of the UN implied that as far as the political situation went, nothing would change in the area. Those people on that territory had to abide by the laws --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- throughout this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry. You'll need to help me on this one. You're in charge of the army at this point, and you don't know if this is what actually happened. I find that strange. Perhaps you could clarify it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were discussing the adoption of the Vance Plan here. As regards to specific issues referring not only to the army but to the entire economy, we agreed that this should all be regulated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't divert attention from the issue. The issue's the army. That's what the question's about. It's not about anything else. It's not about anything else. And the question's very specific. It's described by you as a concrete issue. And the question is about transferring 20.000 men to the police, and were you prepared for Adzic and Kadijevic not to order and to pull out the tanks, because "we won't give them," and you say that would be cheaper for Serbia and Montenegro as an option. You're in charge of the army. Are you saying you don't know whether that actually happened or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, what we were discussing here, we said that these issues would be solved by the relevant ministries. So what was mentioned regarding the army had to be resolved with the Ministry of Defence. Whether 20.000 men were left there or not, I don't know, but as regards tanks and artillery, I can tell you that we didn't manage to pull out a single piece of weaponry from the Muslim territories in Bosnia or from the Croatian territories simply because it was the people, the Muslim and the Croat people respectively that stood in front of those weapons and we couldn't run over the people. That's my response to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but the anxiety for me, Mr. Kostic, is if you don't know the answer to this sort of question, I have to ask myself whether, when you do give detailed answers about the behaviour of the army, you're actually speaking from genuine knowledge or not, because this seems quite an important matter and one on which I would have thought the member of the Presidency with responsibility for the army would have known.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what can I tell you now, Mr. Bonomy? You can doubt the truthfulness of my testimony, that's all. After 15 years -- maybe if I had time I could find out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And learn how many policemen were left in Krajina, how many were funded, but I can't answer that question now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps the question could be put a different way: Did you know at the time, and have you now forgotten? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had I known then and forgotten in the meantime, well, I'd probably still know it today had I known then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, what's the point in pointing out to me that it's 15 years ago? I'm not following this reaction to this line of questioning. But anyway, let's let the Prosecutor continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I cannot remember that right now. I can't answer that question, quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Are you aware that after -- after the Vance Plan was actually -- after the Vance Plan was agreed upon, that afterwards the -- there was a strong cooperation between the JNA and the later army of the RSK? Are you aware of the strong cooperation financially, in staffing and the like?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what you're referring to now. I only know that when the peace forces of the UN arrived, we withdrew the JNA completely from the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to tender this -- this document. Mr. Milosevic didn't, but I would like to tender it as a Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kostic, in relation to the Vance Plan and violations of the Vance Plan, Mr. Milosevic asked you about violations of the Vance Plan, and you said actually that exclusively the paramilitary formations of Croatia violated the agreement, and I would like to put to you now a report of the Security Council on that situation of the 27th of July, 1992, and it's Defence Exhibit -- it's D94, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, don't try. On the 15th I withdrew from political life and from the government, and you're saying this was on the 27th of July, 1992. I won't be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This report relates to actually the period passing -- that passed since the establishment of the Vance Plan. It's not something that happens on the 27th of July, Mr. Kostic, but it's a report about the time period that has passed since February 1992. Therefore, I think you will be able to answer my questions. But let me put this to you and -- first of all --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have this report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let it be passed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It is Defence Exhibit D94, and of course we have a copy for you -- for Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And I quote first from paragraph 5 here, point 5. It says here: "Prior to the UNPROFOR's assumption of responsibility in the UNPAs, it had become apparent that the JNA was transferring many of its heavy weapons to local Territorial Defence units and paramilitary militias established in these areas. The Force Commander has informed me that all TO units in Sectors East and West have handed over their heavy weapons and that these weapons, which include tanks, artillery, mortars, and anti-aircraft weapons systems, have been stored ..." and so on and so forth. Mr. Kostic, what the UNPROFOR commanders found out is exactly what you were talking about with the Croatian Serbs that we just talked about; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you read at the end is what I keep saying. The JNA complied with the Vance Plan completely. All heavy weapons were stored in depots. You can see that for yourselves now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I've just read to you the opposite. The commander of the UNPROFOR found out that before they came, JNA transferred heavy weapons to the TO. That's just what we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And paramilitary militias, according to this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They found out, although they didn't have a list, obviously. They found out.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you have anywhere in these UN reports that this was misused, or were these weapons stored quite properly?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You don't -- so you -- I understand you don't want to answer my question. It's a very simple question. I read to you what the UNPROFOR commanders found out, and that's what really happened; right? Before they came, weapons were transferred from the JNA to the TO so that they could stay in the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't be able to give you a specific answer. I don't exclude the possibility, because we had a lot of problems trying to convince the people there to accept the Blue Helmets. All the weapons left for them were left for their protection and for their security. I was not informed of any complaints that these weapons which were stored there were misused by members of the Territorial Defence or the police on the territory of Serbian Krajina. The depots were opened only when the paramilitary formations of Croatia attempted to penetrate into these protected areas again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I move on to paragraph 7. In paragraph 7 of this same report it says the following: "However, the process of demobilisation of the TO forces in the sectors has been complicated by the parallel emergence of strengthened police and militia organisations. These groups, designed as 'Special police,' 'Border police' and so on are equipped with automatic rifles and, in some cases, with machine-guns, in violation of the provisions of the plan which require that the police be equipped only with sidearms. In many cases these groups have taken over from the JNA or the Serb Territorial Defence force's responsibility for manning the front lines; they will have to be withdrawn and disbanded. These matters have been repeatedly taken up with the local authorities, but so far without satisfactory results." Mr. Kostic, what the UN is complaining about is that the Serb side violated the Vance Plan. That's correct, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that what you are reading out, some parallel units taking over something from the JNA means that the JNA was no longer there. If it's correct that the JNA was no longer there, then our responsibility in those territories no longer existed. Those were territories where there was neither Yugoslav authority nor Croatian authority. The areas were under the control of the United Nations. If such things did occur, it was up to the UN to intervene. We were no longer competent. We were no longer responsible.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, when you talked with Mr. Milosevic, you said that only the Croats violated the Vance Plan agreement, and I'm putting to you now complaints by the UN that the Serb side violated the agreement, and do I have to understand you didn't know that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, you should not assume. I'm telling you you're reading a UN report of the 27th of July when I had already completely withdrawn from political life. This is the first time I've heard this report. On the 15th of June, I handed over the duty of president to Dobrica Cosic, president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and I retired.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'll stop you. I read now paragraph 14 of that report, only part of it about expulsion, coercion, and intimidation, and this is what is in the report: "In earlier cases, especially before an UNPROFOR assumption of responsibility, these expulsions were carried out in a blatant manner." It's hard to read. "Families were, under physical threat, gathered from their houses in buses and trucks and transported to areas outside the UNPAs. This had been most evident in Sector East. Since assuming its responsibilities, UNPROFOR has been able, as a result of intense patrolling and control of checkpoints, to put a stop to mass expulsions. Individual cases of intimidation resulting in the forced departure of persons from their homes have, however, continued to occur ..." Mr. Kostic, they are speaking here from a time period in which UNPROFOR wasn't there yet and you were still in the Presidency. What do you say to this, the mass expulsion of non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you, madam. As regards mass expulsion, I can assert with certainty that the JNA, that we were responsible for, expelled no one. There was an inter-ethnic and inter-religious conflict there. Wherever there are such conflicts, the population of both ethnicities and religious affiliations flees and goes to places where they will feel physically more secure. You're saying that even after UNPROFOR took over there were individual threats and so on. But even if this was the case and even if it had been the case before UNPROFOR arrived, could I have been informed of everything that happened on that territory between those people who were waging a civil war? That's why I'm asking you, when will you start indicting Mr. Blair for all the murders and rapes that happened in London last night?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to move on now to an entirely different issue, and it's just one question that I have to you in relation to the retiring -- retiring of officers. And we have heard a great deal about this, and I don't want to go into any details. I just want to refer to your book, actually, your book "1991, Not To Be Forgotten." This is Defence Exhibit D333, tab 72. And I would like to have this provided to everyone. It's page 108 in your book, and we have a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, when are you proposing to conclude?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In the next session, Your Honour. Sometime in the next session. I have actually only two more complex items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: As much as I do not like the time counting, you are beyond the two-thirds limit.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, he is very -- and at this point I agree with Mr. Milosevic: Mr. Kostic is a very important witness in this case. He's actually the one who was at the head of the state at that time, and therefore I would like to cover a few more aspects, and it would -- I assume that there will be some redirect, and I assume that this will -- by the end of that, it will be the two-thirds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, but be as brief as possible in the next session.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In relation to the retiring of officers, I would like to refer you to your book, and it says here on page 108 --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you tell me the page number again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 108. 108, and it's actually marked also in the document provided to you by the usher. I don't want to read the whole conversation, what you have mentioned here, but the only thing I would like to quote is you say here: "That same evening, a little while after Adzic's telephone call, Slobodan Milosevic called me. He was angry. He specifically criticised me because General Marko Negovanovic's name was included in the list of retired generals," and then in brackets there is the sentence: "Slobodan Milosevic and Momir Bulatovic did not have insight into the whole list." And my question is what do you mean by saying they "did not have insight into the whole list"? What does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that several months previously, the Federal Secretariat for National Defence had provided us with a complete list of all the generals of the JNA, classified into several groups. Two groups were of special interest and the reason we asked for the list was that we wanted to know which were the generals which, pursuant to the law, either because their years of service or because of their age, fulfilled the conditions for retirement. As I've already said, we had a huge number of generals. It was too big even for the old Yugoslavia, the entire Yugoslavia. Now that Yugoslavia was reduced in size by half, the number of generals was far too large and had to be reduced.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We do not need to have it all repeated. I only asked you was there a list that Mr. Milosevic should have had but didn't have? This is how I would read your remark, "insight into the whole list."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Presidency had the list. Neither Mr. Milosevic nor Mr. Bulatovic had it. It was the Presidency that had the list. This was taking place when Mr. Jovic was going to China. We consulted everyone we had to consult. We were not doing anything simply on our own initiative, although Mr. Jovic said that this was impudence on my part. I never asked him why he described it in this way, nor will I, but I have explained why Mr. Milosevic should have known about Mr. Marko Negovanovic. Mr. Marko Negovanovic was not pensioned off as the Serbian minister of defence but only as a general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, we're going to take the break for 20 minutes. We are adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps could that be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to have now a bit from Mr. Kostic's book put in front of him, and the page is 47 and 48. It's Defence Exhibit 333, tab 72. Mr. Kostic, you have already addressed the Belgrade Initiative with Mr. Milosevic, and I do not want to go into any details of that. Only one question, and that relates to the page 47 in your book, and the chapter is marked.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's on the first page of the translation that you should have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: You say here: "This is because Momir Bulatovic and Slobodan Milosevic were the co-authors of the so-called Belgrade Initiative." Is that so? Were they the co-authors of the Belgrade Initiative? Just a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And a little bit further down on that same page in your book, you say the following: "Therefore, I expressed my opinion that despite all --"

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not receiving the interpretation. No interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let's try again.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In your book, a little bit further down, just a few lines further down, it says --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all right now.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- "Therefore, I expressed my opinion that despite all, Momir Bulatovic should be kept on because I feared that with his dismissal the conflict might spread into Montenegro." Mr. Kostic, does that mean at that time when Mr. Bulatovic had actually agreed to the Carrington Plan and also had made an attempt to withdraw Montenegrin soldiers from the front line, that Mr. Milosevic, Jovic, and you discussed his dismissal?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't discuss his dismissal at all. What it was about was that I, as representative of Montenegro and vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, assumed one position and Mr. Momir Bulatovic, as president of Montenegro, quite another position at The Hague conference. And knowing the mood prevailing in Montenegro, that the population was even then fiercely divided in two different polls over those options, I knew that there would be a great deal of reaction amongst the population. And in that sense, I told Jovic and Mr. Milosevic -- we travelled together, we sat together and talked -- I expressed the view that everything should be done to keep Momir Bulatovic, that is to say not to open a new conflict between me and him in Montenegro because we had a lot of difficulties to deal with of a difficult nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one thing in relation to the Belgrade Initiative. Mr. Milosevic and Mr. Kostic had discussed it alongside the Defence Exhibit D333, tab 84, and it was then not admitted because Judge -- His Honour Judge Kwon pointed out that the Belgrade Initiative document was already admitted under another exhibit number, namely 338, tab 9. However, 338, tab 9, was only a basic proposal with a few points, and the provisions discussed between Mr. Kostic and Mr. Milosevic are actually quite complex, and they are not yet in evidence. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I mentioned another tab number, didn't I? D272.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Then my information is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was informed that tab 84 was not yet -- this document was not yet admitted. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're a brave person, anyhow, to take on Judge Kwon on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know how this comes about. We have already in evidence, and I would like to put this to Mr. Kostic, the article, Epoha article dealing with the convention on the new Yugoslavia, and it's Exhibit 808. And could that be put to Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the convention on new Yugoslavia held in the SFRY parliament on the 3rd of January, 1992. And, Mr. Kostic, was that an initiative by the SFRY Presidency, this convention?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In the text here that is before us, it says that the initiative for holding the convention on a third Yugoslavia came from several political parties from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the initiative board made up of, I think, nine political parties of Bosnia-Herzegovina came to the Yugoslav state Presidency. We agreed to hold a meeting. They came, and we in the Presidency accepted being the sponsors of the meeting. So it was the -- under the auspices of the SFRY Presidency that that convention was held.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And on page 4 of the English translation, there is a reference to: "The process of building a new Yugoslavia will definitely depend on the will of the nation, citizens, and republics that want to join it." And it says -- it lists here those who want to join. "So far, Serbia and Montenegro, Republic of Serbian Krajina, and Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that includes autonomous regions -" they're listed then here - "have declared one way or another that they want to stay in the new federal state." The representatives of these entities, they were all present; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but mostly they were from Bosnia-Herzegovina. The vast majority, in fact, was from Bosnia-Herzegovina. But there were representatives of political parties, associations, movements from other parts of Yugoslavia as well who had expressed the desire to stay within Yugoslavia. And in tab 72 in my book, you will find a comprehensive list of all the participants in the convention, and there were 109 of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kostic. And on page 5 of the English translation there, it says in the middle of this page: "Pursuant to the convention on new Yugoslavia, the SFRY Assembly has to bring decisions that will enable overall solution of the Yugoslav political crisis, including decisions on conditions and procedure for realisation of the right of a nation to self-determination and decisions on criteria and principles that would be a base for a just, territorial, and material separation between new Yugoslavia and the parts of the former SFRY where the peoples want to create independent and sovereign states outside of Serbia." Mr. Kostic, does that mean territorial separation and drawing new borders between those new independent states and the new Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you would have to ask the authors of this Declaration, of this Declaration on the New Yugoslavia, the third Yugoslavia that was adopted at that meeting. There were representatives from all over. And at the convention, we also discussed the protectorate, UN protectorate of the Serbian Krajinas in Croatia and to seek solutions for the position of that nation over there. Now, as far as Yugoslavia was concerned, and this is the 3rd of January, those of us who really did strive to preserve Yugoslavia from the very first day, even in a reduced form, that is to say without Slovenia and Croatia, at the time we still believed, and I particularly believed, that we would succeed in keeping Bosnia within the frameworks of the reduced Yugoslavia. And all our thoughts went along those lines. We didn't expect the Muslims in Bosnia to turn against the Serbs and that a civil war should break out there, although that was always a concern.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: When you now say that you were still considering Bosnia to be part of this, I would like to put the map that was actually related to the convention of the new Yugoslavia on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, you have it also. It's part of this Epoha article, but it's in black and white. Yes. I would like you to have the coloured version of this map. And it's -- but I have to tell you that it's only in B/C/S here. The coloured version, we have the B/C/S names of all the territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I think we do not need to concern ourself with that, Mr. Kostic. This map attached to the new Yugoslavia, the convention of Yugoslavia of the 3rd of January, that's not including the entire Bosnia. It's actually including the Serb territories only; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say first of all that this is the first time that I see this map. I didn't see this map at the Convention on Yugoslavia. And here what I can notice is that in the explanations given, it wasn't a map of the new Yugoslavia but what it says here is that they were the regions whose population had already declared themselves in favour of staying in Yugoslavia. That's what it says in the map as well. The map whose population has already declared itself willing to remain within Yugoslavia. As far as I remember, the Muslims and Croats later on, after the convention on the new Yugoslavia, organised a referendum, and it was at the referendum that they came out contrary to the constitution and contrary to the law, that they wanted a sovereign state, that is to say without the participation of the Serb people and without the participation of deputies in the Serbian Assembly and members of the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, Macedonia, too, is in the shaded area. So it was still not the option to remain within Yugoslavia. All we have here is the territories whose population said they wanted to remain within Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: However, the fact is that this wasn't a component part of the convention, this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to put to you now a map, and it's another map. It's Exhibit 809A. It's a coloured map. And just very briefly, Mr. Kostic, it's a coloured map indicating the Serb-held territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina in December 1992. And just have a look at it. And would you agree that those little blue dots along the -- this blue -- this blue separate sections along the border with Serbia, Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, where the Muslims were in the majority, and would you agree to this? Can you read that map this way?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I see this map for the first time, just like the one you showed us the previous time. You say the 30th of December, 1992. I don't know. From the aspects of how far I am acquainted with the relief and the map of the former Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, I can only assume that the blue areas near the border with Serbia are areas -- represent areas which might be Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica. That is possible. That's where they should be, somewhere in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And in the middle of the actually Serb-controlled areas, more to the Croatian border, there is also a dark blue Muslim area indicated. That's Bihac; right?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that is Bihac, but let me state again this is the first time that I see this map, and dating back to those times I really can't tell you anything. I can't be of assistance here. But once again, from the aspects of the geography of the former Yugoslavia, I would say that that area was the Muslim part where Mr. Fikret Abdic was and where he had formed his autonomous Muslim region. But I don't think that is the area of Bihac. I think it is more to the north-west of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And we see something --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
