utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff is asking the witness about things that she has not established in the first place. She hasn't said what they are. He said that it wasn't a document that was used at the convention in Yugoslavia, and it was indeed not. If it is a map taken from some newspaper, then I'm wondering what sense there is in asking the witness that, because different newspapers wrote different things, all sorts of things. So what is the sense of asking the witness about a map that was drawn perhaps by some newspaper? Or she can tell us what the document is. Whose document it is, the provenance the document, and then go ahead and ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, are you still on the map?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I'm not on the map from the newspaper, actually. I have said that this is a map used as Exhibit 89 -- 809, and it is actually, as it says here, it's from the UNPROFOR map. It says here: "Source: Front lines in Bosnia and Herzegovina are from an UNPROFOR map and shows status as of 30 December 1992."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. And what is your next question?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: My next question was related to that small corridor that is here between the areas along the Drina and the other Serb areas, and my question to you was: When these areas were actually inhabited by mostly Muslims, and in relation to the corridor, mostly Muslims and Croats, why did the Serbs try to get it? Why was all this fighting about in the years from 1992 to 1995? Can you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I could give you my opinion in answer to your question in the extent in which an average citizen slightly better informed about it or in view of the positions I held could tell you, but I don't know whether there's any sense of giving you my opinion here in view of the fact that --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to -- wanted to know from you if you can help us with this in relation to your -- you were in a position -- you were in a very important position until mid of 1992, and the question is: Do you -- can you give us any facts that could actually answer this question that I was addressing: Why did the Serbs try to capture these areas where the Muslims and the Croats were in the majority? That was my question. Do you know? Can you help us with facts in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, madam, you yourself said that it was the period from 1992 to 1995, and in June 1992 I'd already left all my positions and posts, and I can just tell you what I said in the examination-in-chief: That the overall civil war, which was a very bloody civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was waged between all three ethnic groups, was a war for territory between all those three nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic -- Mr. Kostic, sorry. I was looking at the book of Mr. Jovic. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: First of all, Your Honour, I forgot - and that's a reminder from Ms. Dicklich - I forgot to ask you to admit the Kostic book, pages 47 to 48 that were previously discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And could the witness please be given from Exhibit 596, tab 2, the Jovic book on "The End of the SFRY," the entry of the 30th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, it's from the book, and it refers to a meeting, a conversation with the Serb leadership from Bosnia and Herzegovina on the 30th of April, 1992, and according to Mr. Jovic's note, you were also present as was Mr. Milosevic. And it says here in this entry, which is a short one: "It is being demanded that we withdraw the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Slobodan and I both expected and predicted this." And a little bit further down, it says: "The problem is that Branko Kostic recently stated recklessly that he, as vice-president of the SFRY Presidency, would never sign an order on withdrawing the JNA --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We're not following.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's in this entry of 30 April 1992, and it's in the third paragraph or, rather, on page 400; and the translation it's the second paragraph. The paragraph starts: "With the withdrawal of the 10 to 15 per cent ..." but I had skipped that and just moved on to the next sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: "The problem is that Branko Kostic ..." "The problem is that Branko Kostic recently stated recklessly that he, as vice-president of the SFRY Presidency, will never sign an order on withdrawing the JNA from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also that Milan Panic stated that the military will not be withdrawn from Bosnia-Herzegovina for five to seven years ..." Mr. Kostic, do you recall this meeting with the Bosnian Serbs attending where you were basically --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do remember that, yes. I remember that. But what you've just quoted from Mr. Jovic's book, I have to say that that is once again something that Mr. Jovic has fabricated. It seems that he was following what my political opponents in Montenegro were saying and what they were criticising me for rather than what we were discussing. My exact words, which are quoted here erroneously, was that never as vice-president of Yugoslav state Presidency would I sign the withdrawal of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia-Herzegovina until the leadership of all three ethnic groups agreed to that. So that is the comprehensive statement that I made. My political components made use of the first part of that statement and omitted the second part of that statement, just like Mr. Jovic omitted the second part of the statement. In my book I go on to explain this, and I say that the Muslim and Croatian leaderships in Bosnia-Herzegovina had already ceased sending young men to the JNA. They had set up their own paramilitary units, and the leadership of the Serbian people in Bosnia accused us of --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you. I was actually --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just complete my thought, with your permission?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like only to discuss this meeting with you, and you have already explained that Mr. Jovic has not cited you fully, and we can leave it at that. But the meeting, you remember it, I understand from your answer. And Mr. Jovic wrote about this meeting, and it's further -- a few lines down, the next paragraph, Your Honours. He says: "Independently of Kostic's and Panic's statements, we discussed the need to withdraw the remainder of soldiers who are FRY citizens from Bosnia-Herzegovina. Even without them, there remain around 90.000 JNA soldiers in that republic, mostly of Serb nationality, over whom the Serb leadership from Bosnia-Herzegovina can resume political command." And then it says: "Karadzic agrees. Krajisnik raises a series of questions: How will that military be financed, who will pay its wages, who will provide its pensions -" and so on and so forth - "all of which are indeed problems, but are not critical to our discussion." Do you recall this being discussed and these questions that Mr. Krajisnik raised?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I really don't remember what it was that Mr. Krajisnik actually said, but I do remember the meeting very well. And as you can see, it was a meeting of the 30th of April when the Security Council had already recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. So this meeting was on the 30th of April when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had already been constituted. And we then met with the leadership of the Bosnian Serbs because previously it had accused us of keeping back or retaining a large number of Serb representatives in the JNA and said that they were weakened by this because, as opposed to the Muslim and Croatian paramilitaries in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the JNA was rather restrained. And so it was quite natural that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe the Prosecutor was interested in whether you remembered any questions about the financing and who will pay the wages of the soldiers, who will provide pensions and so on. Do you have any recollection of that kind of discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't recollect that part of the discussion, but I do remember very well what we agreed on at the time and what we actually did and undertook, and that was to finally withdraw the JNA from Bosnia and Herzegovina, although four days previously Mr. Adzic and I had had a meeting with Mr. Alija Izetbegovic in Skopje. At that meeting, he told us that the army could stay for five years, if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kostic, I would like to put part of your book to you in relation to the JNA withdrawal from Bosnia and Herzegovina. Everyone should get the English translation. And I would actually only like to quote the footnote 85 to pages -- to these pages that you have in front of you, and the footnote is as follows: "At that moment, the Decision of the Presidency of SFRY ... was fully completed in regard to the withdrawal of the units of the JNA from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. "When in December 1991, immediately after Vatican, also Germany, recognised without waiting 15 January 1992 as the date agreed in the European Community, it was clear to us that Germany would do everything to get recognition of independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In such anticipated situation, the JNA in Bosnia and Herzegovina would be treated by the international community as an aggressor army on the territory of a foreign state. "That is why, in February 1992, the Supreme Command ordered the General Staff to redeploy military conscripts serving with the Yugoslav People's Army in the shortest possible period by bringing all the military conscripts from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina who were serving in the Yugoslav People's Army in the territories of Serbia, Macedonia, and Montenegro back to their home republics. We did not have any legal basis to force JNA officers and non-commissioned officers originally from Bosnia and Herzegovina to return to Bosnia and Herzegovina ... However, we left the possibility open of allowing all these military officers who volunteered to be deployed in the JNA in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina to do it. This measure was implemented swiftly. Therefore, in April 1992, when the Presidency took the Decision on the JNA withdrawal from Bosnia and Herzegovina, it only had to withdraw, from Bosnia and Herzegovina, 15 per cent of the total number of troops ..." and so forth. This was how it was; is that right? This is what you wrote here.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And do you know and were you involved in solving the matters that Mr. Krajisnik raised, that is the payment of the JNA officers that remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina? Do you know that they were paid, continued to be paid through the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that this was regulated with the responsible Secretariat for National Defence and that the JNA was duty-bound to pay pensions to its employees who had done their years of service in the JNA. However, the interview you are quoting from is an interview from May 1992. At this meeting that you mentioned on the 13th of April, Mr. Krajisnik raised this issue. I can only assume what happened, but I'm really not informed. I assume that this was regulated with the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, which was responsible for this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Do you know about a 30th Personnel Centre in relation to the payment of the officers that remained in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing this for the first time. I don't really know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to have this footnote admitted as part of this tab 72.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you have discussed crime bases with Mr. Milosevic during the examination-in-chief, and you basically more or less said that you wouldn't know those kind of things. However, you, in a position as the member of the Presidency, you received information from the JNA, did you not, about what was going on in the territories?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did receive information. I think the staff of the Supreme Command or the General Staff of the JNA frequently issued public communiques, mentioning the number of men killed, the number of truces broken, and so on and so forth. But these communiques had to do with the involvement and the activities of the paramilitary formations of Croatia and the activities of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you said actually in the examination-in-chief - and that is at transcript page 48054 to 56 - you actually said that you had regular briefings by the JNA and you toured the war zones and thus knew about all the activities of the JNA. Is that -- do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say that's what I said verbatim, it's possible. I may have been incautious, but I don't think I said we knew everything. But it's true that we did receive information and that we did tour the areas. I don't think I was so incautious as to say that. If I was, I have to correct myself. Of course I wasn't able to know everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I actually had quoted you as you said it. In relation to the crimes of which you say you didn't know about it, I just wanted to refer you to some documents that definitely must have reached you, because they're basically addressed to you or the Presidency. And first of all I refer here to Exhibit 330, tab 68. And it's a strong protest by the government of the Republic of Croatia to, inter alia, the Presidency of the SFRY, of the 25th of July, 1991. And in this document, they complain about an event on the 25th of July, 1991, in which members of the JNA opened artillery and tank fire on the villages of Erdut and Bogojevci in the Republic of Croatia. What did you do about it, Mr. Kostic, when you received this?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that at that time in that one-year period, there were quite a few protests by the government of the Republic of Croatia and that we had different information respecting many of these from the staff of the General Command. I really don't remember this specific case, but if I were to go through the documents carefully, I might remember. However, at present I can't say anything specific about it. I see that they are mentioning Erdut and Bogojevci. If I'm not mistaken - I don't know if this is the period of the Ohrid Declaration - it might be that this is when we were in Ohrid, but I can't be sure. I do know that there was a lot of provocation, ways and means of a sort for Mr. President Tudjman to walk out of the Ohrid meeting so that we had the Ohrid Declaration practically without him. But I can't tell you more about this without going through the documents in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it's a fact that you -- that Mr. Mesic and the Croats, in writing and also during Presidency session, would talk about what they call attacks by the JNA and by those local forces. That's -- so you had some information to this effect, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, Mr. Mesic publicly attacked his own army, the one of which he was the Commander-in-Chief, saying that they were using --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- toxic materials and poisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, it was a simple question. I just asked you, you got this information from Mr. Mesic and through letters from the Croatian government, and you -- do I have to understand your answer to mean you didn't deal with it because you didn't believe it, or what position did you take?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A large proportion of this information was incorrect, madam. When we received information, we usually tasked a working group. Usually it was Mr. Vasil Tupurkovski and Bogic Bogicevic who were tasked with investigating. And a large proportion of this information was incorrect. I can't tell you anything specific about this particular instance without going through all the documents and seeing what this is actually all about. I would even have to look at these reports drawn up by these working groups tasked to investigate whether a crime had or had not been committed somewhere. You can't expect me to know about each specific instance now, 15 years after these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we also have here, and that's at tab -- Exhibit 359, tab 3, that is a letter of Helsinki Watch of the 21st of January, 1992. It's a letter to Mr. Milosevic and General Adzic in which they list various crimes that had been committed in these conflict areas in Croatia, and my question to you is, as it goes to General Adzic, did -- do you know this letter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you got a copy in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually an English -- it's a letter written by Helsinki Watch, and it's in English. It's from the committee in New York. So do you know the letter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But as for the Helsinki Watch, I can say throughout the time I was holding government posts they had already decided in advance who were the good guys and who were the bad guys in the Yugoslav crisis.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have a copy of the letter, Mr. Robinson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But I didn't intend to go now into details. As you said, you do not know this letter, and even if you had got it, you wouldn't really believe it to be correct. Is that what you say, Mr. Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please don't interpret my ideas in your own way. All I said was that at the time while I was holding government posts in Belgrade for a year, the Helsinki Watch was prominent among those who had already decided in advance who were going to be the good guys and who the bad guys in the Yugoslav war. However, I'm not familiar with the content of this letter, so I can't talk about it in advance.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, now another letter, and that's tab -- Exhibit 643.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, this exhibit that I now will put to him, it's a letter from UNESCO to Mr. Kostic, and it was addressed in Exhibit 643, tab 1. That's the report of Mr. Theunens, but this document was not admitted -- it was not tendered separately with the report. And I would like to have Mr. Kostic look at it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, it's a letter of the 25th October 1991. It's about concerns that UNESCO has in relation to old city -- inter alia, the Old City of Dubrovnik. Do you -- did you receive this letter?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At present I don't remember receiving this letter, but as it's addressed to me and in view of its contents and in view of our involvement at the time in October in securing and protecting Dubrovnik and other national and cultural heritage sites, I assume that it did reach me, but I don't really remember this particular letter. I do know, however, that at the time we were paying a lot of attention to protecting cultural monuments and the national heritage, especially with respect to Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What did you do? This is just a very general remark. What did you instruct the JNA in relation to -- to do in relation to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that in the documentation. On more than one occasion, as the Presidency, we drew the fact that the cultural heritage had to be protected. I even visited the Dubrovnik. To be sure, I couldn't visit the Old Town at the time, but I did visit in mid-October, even before the arrival of this letter, and I also know that the staff of the Supreme Command issued warnings to lower-ranking commands and units, saying that the Old Town in Dubrovnik had to be preserved and not destroyed. I think the Old Town was preserved. As for damage in Dubrovnik, which wasn't very serious, it occurred on those buildings which were used as firing points threatening the JNA. Dubrovnik was used by the media.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you the source of your information that there were firing points within the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had occasion to see some footage about the destruction in the Old Town and reports from the diplomatic corps which toured the Old Town. I was also able to see some original film footage of an archival nature. This was original footage from -- from the territory where the JNA units were. A journalist was asking a private, who was in a trench, why they weren't advancing - and you can see that this is not staged - and he says, "Well, we would advance but there is some kind of botanical garden down there and they're not allowing us to shoot at it." I know for certain that the General Staff issued a special order that JNA units should not approach Dubrovnik and the Old Town close enough to be threatened from the Old Town. But I also know that, under those conditions, when a state of war had not been declared, there certainly was lack of discipline among individual lower-ranking units approaching the town and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't really think you've answered my question, have you? What was the source of your information that there were firing points within the Old Town? Forget facility for answering a different question from the one that's actually asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the sources was the archive film on the Dubrovnik operation, which I have with me if you're interested. It will show you. It's the Arkitel [phoen] film on the Dubrovnik operation, where seven or eight inhabitants of Dubrovnik speak, among them the commander of the defence of Dubrovnik and a Croatian journalist. I am the only interlocutor in the film on our side. And the film shows very clearly, first of all, that the army did not have the intention of taking the town; secondly, that the artillery pieces used were not heavy pieces, they were light mortars. Furthermore, that the town was not that badly damaged. It was just misused in the media to accuse the JNA and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you don't have an answer to my question. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same film I'm telling you about shows that several palazzos in the Old Town were destroyed but the Old Town is very big, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You see, Mr. Kostic, you're constantly telling me about how little firing was done at Dubrovnik, and I understand your position on that. What I'm trying to find out is the source of your information that parts of the Old Town of Dubrovnik were the source of firing at the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I've just told you is knowledge I gained later on, looking at this archive film, for example, on the Dubrovnik operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. I've taken up enough time on this unproductive exercise.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, we have heard here in this court a lot of evidence that on the 6th of December, 1991, Dubrovnik, the Old Town, was heavily shelled and actually that there was heavy damage, in particular on certain palazzi, as you say, and in particular the roofs. Do you dispute that? Are you still now, after so many years of information, do you still claim Dubrovnik wasn't really attacked on that day? Old Town.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have stated this in public more than once, and I say so in Arkitel's film on the Dubrovnik operation. It's only when I heard the testimonies at this Tribunal when individual citizens of Dubrovnik testified that I learned about the 6th of December as something special, when there was especially heavy shelling by the JNA. But until that time, I really knew nothing about it. I have had occasion to hear information from the staff of the naval district denying such claims made by Croatian propaganda, and it was only during the trials here that I was able to hear about these details. And pursuant to what I learnt, I don't deny those.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I forgot to ask for the admission of this UNESCO letter to Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit 952.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in Sanction, I would like to play now a video. And the interpreters should know that it is Exhibit 365. It's already admitted, Your Honours, but I would like to put this to Mr. Kostic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] Distinguished viewers, good evening. And Montenegrin President Milan Djukanovic expressed his commiserations to the Croatian --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, but we are unable to find the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] ... the afternoon the Cavtat meeting of Stipe Mesic and Mile Djukanovic, which was a tete-a-tete meeting, is the first high level meeting since the aggression on Croatia. It is the result of both sides' initiatives. The talks went on for about an hour. And as President Mesic said, many questions were opened but also closed. "I should like to take this opportunity in my own name and also on behalf of the citizens of Montenegro, especially those citizens who share my moral and political convictions, to say that I deeply regret, and my sympathies with all the citizens of the Republic of Croatia, especially the citizens of Konavle, Dubrovnik, for all the pain and all the suffering and all the material losses and damages that were inflicted on them by any representative of the Montenegrin people within the Yugoslav People's Army. "Mesic and Djukanovic assess today's meeting as ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, why did Mr. Djukanovic -- why did he actually apologise? I mean, would you join this apology?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, why Mr. Djukanovic apologised, you'd have to ask him that, the reason for that. Now, what I would have done - and I can say this quite openly and frankly - is this: I'm very sorry for all the sufferings and casualties during that tragic 1991/1992 year on all sides, and I have -- feel great pain because of all these casualties and sufferings. But if there was somebody who would be best placed to apologise, it would be Mr. Stjepan Mesic, without counting the other two men who would have to apologise to the Serb people for the mass exodus that took place, the largest exodus of the Serb people after World War II, in fact. So that's my political opinion, you know. Mr. Demikalis [phoen] once asked me, in saying that his greatest contribution was that Mr. Bulatovic had accepted The Hague document, also assessed him as being a stubborn politician, not ready to enter into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kostic. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let's, yes. Your Honour, I would like to put a map to the witness that actually was produced in the Office of the Prosecutor, and it is actually depicting the crime bases in the Croatia indictment. Only -- we have listed here only the murders and the killings -- the killings in red, and the detention facilities in blue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kostic, you have already mentioned that you wouldn't know about the details of the detention facilities, so we would not have to deal with this. In relation to the killing incidents that you see here shown in this map, I would like you first of all to look at the left -- the right-hand corner with this huge group of incidents, the red boxes, and it all relates to Eastern Slavonia around the Erdut region. And this high concentration of killings, they're actually always involving Arkan and his men, and Vukovar, Lovas, and a few other crimes. Do you claim that you don't know any of these -- anything about these crimes committed by Arkan?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, let me correct you on one point. As far as these facilities are concerned where the people were gathered or detained, the prisoners, in the examination-in-chief I just took note of what it said in the indictment, that where those facilities were mentioned you can see that they were military facilities.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I didn't ask you -- I actually said that I'm not addressing the detention facilities because you have already mentioned that you couldn't help us with this. But I ask you about these killing counts that we have here related to Erdut, Dalj, and I would -- I put to you whether you really claim and uphold today that you know nothing about Arkan killing people in that area. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Give us a short answer, Mr. Kostic. Don't digress.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said during the examination-in-chief that these details about killings and crimes that took place, I don't know. I can't speak about them. I don't know about them. And I already said, as far as Arkan's forces are concerned, I don't know where they were located or if they were present. All I knew was that Seselj and the radicals provided volunteers who made up the JNA and Territorial Defence units.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I would like to put to the witness now a document from the 1st Military District that is addressed to the military command, and it's of the 18th of October, 1991. And it should be provided to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, this is now a military commander, Major General Mile Babic. He is writing to Mr. Kadijevic's office, speaking of unauthorised killings of arrested ZNG members and other individuals, and he in particular refers to killings from October 1991 committed by Raznjatovic Arkan and the special police in Dalj commanded by Stricevic Milorad, and they are committing unauthorised killings of arrested ZNG members, arresting Croatian individuals, and committing certain acts against the same. Now that it is -- and they refer to a particular killing of a certain Stjepan Pap. And as this is going to the security administration of the SSNO, I wonder whether you know this, this document or the allegations that are in this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please, this is the first time that I see this. I said that the counter-intelligence service and KOS was subordinate to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, that it was under that and not the Presidency as the Supreme Command, and this is the first time I see this document and I am quite certain that it never reached the Presidency. But these kinds of reports probably exist on the Croatian side as well and on the Yugoslav side, and there were tonnes of things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just asked you whether you got information, this information, and your answer is no. I could put now many more of similar documents to you where the security services actually are addressing crimes committed by Serbs, Serb units, or Arkan or similar groups in the territory of the former -- territory of Croatia, and your answer would be you never -- did you never receive any of those information? Did it never reach you?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the most responsible officers, the top officers from the staff did inform us that there were paramilitaries, that there were individual crimes that were happening over there, and so on the basis of that kind of report to the effect that there were paramilitaries there, paramilitary armies, that nobody was controlling, that didn't listen to anyone, we at the Supreme Command would make special conclusions and tell the staff of the Supreme Command that all the armed formations on those territories should be placed under its control and that paramilitaries should be disbanded and sent home, disarmed and sent home. But detailed information of this kind, as I've already said, you would probably find tonnes of documents like this on both sides. So I neither have them nor did I receive them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I need to put more. I have an abundance of documents to put to the witness of that similar nature where information actually was presented, but I -- as I see, I have no time to do this. Can this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Was this the first one that you put?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, it's the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Put one more.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. And this one is not actually yet an exhibit, Your Honour. I would like to have this admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Oh, he didn't -- he didn't acknowledge --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- your proposition.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, he didn't. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We can't admit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, I withdraw this request.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Let me put to you the documents Exhibit 686.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I am of the opinion that if the Defence is not opposed to it, we can admit it. We can ask him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, are you in opposition to the admission of this document?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot get accustomed to switching my own microphone on and not having somebody else switch it on for me. But I am against it, opposed to it, for reasons of principle. Professor Kostic, who was the vice-president of the Presidency of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's ends it, Mr. Milosevic. If you're opposed to it, we will not admit it because the witness didn't support the propositions put by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Your Honour, one more of these documents. It's already an exhibit, 686, and it is a letter of the chief of security, Milenko Djokovic [phoen], and it's also going to the SSNO security administration, and it's from the 13th of October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And in that letter, in the English it's on the second page, there is mentioning of Serbian guard. "According to our confirmed operational information, a paramilitary formation called 'Serbian Guard' is taking part in combat operations against Ustasha Soldiery carried out in many places in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. A Command has been formed in the Vojvodina TO centre-Erdut and it is headed by Raznjatovic Zeljko, aka Arkan, and a group of his assistants. Mijacic Goran, aka Kum, has a special role there. They (Arkan and Kum) have special attention and privileged treatment by numerous Ministers and other officials of the Serbian Government every day. They are becoming idols of resistance movement of the Serbian people and in reality they represent the corps of the proposed Nationalistic Soldiery, using the motto "For the King and the fatherland. "In the greater area of Vukovar, volunteer troops under the command of Arkan and Kum are committing uncontrolled genocide and various forms of terrorism ..." And a little bit further down, it says: "We estimate that this is a very dangerous and well-organised paramilitary group of considerable power." Mr. Kostic, this is another document from a rather high-ranking official that goes to the SSNO, complaining about Arkan being involved in uncontrolled genocide and forms of terrorism. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document, like the previous one, is one that I see here for the first time, but let me remind you that it says in this document here as a subtitle or, rather, as a title, it says, "The work of the staff of the Serb Guard from Belgrade on the military organisation and breaking up of the armed forces of the SFRY." So this is an intelligence report or, rather, an intelligence organisation is informing about the work of a paramilitary formation which is working to breaking up the armed forces of the SFRY. So this is a piece of information that I am seeing here for the first time, and it was probably the kind of report that we in the Supreme Command were motivated by so that we issue an order to the Supreme Command that all paramilitaries be either placed under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army or to disarm them and disband them and send them home. Otherwise, this document --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But if I understand your answer correctly, it is -- it is possible that you received this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you didn't understand me properly.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: What does it say here, and I quote now: "It was probably the kind of report that we in the Supreme Command were motivated by so that we issued an order to the Supreme Command that all paramilitaries be either placed under the control and the force ..." That sounds to me as if you did receive information of that kind. Perhaps not this particular one but information of that kind.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, you didn't understand me properly, madam, and don't put words that I didn't say into my mouth, or what you would like to hear from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, just answer the question and refrain from those comments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't, Mr. Bonomy, when she's putting things into my mouth that I didn't say. Then you ought to caution the representative of the OTP as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: She only quoted to you what's on the transcript, exactly word-for-word, according to at least the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, she made the wrong conclusion then. I said exactly word-for-word that this piece of information, this report, like the previous document, I had never seen before. Now, she is concluding that I could have received it, so I have to intervene.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, not this particular -- let me correct that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me quote your words again, Professor Kostic. You said as follows: "It was probably the kind of report that we in the Supreme Command were motivated by so that we issue an order to the Supreme Command that all paramilitaries be either placed under the control of the JNA or to disarm them and disband them and send them home." What did you mean by saying, "It was probably the kind of report that we in the Supreme Command were motivated by"?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we can see here that this specific piece of information did not go to the Supreme Command. This report went to the intelligence organ. And as you can see, this is from the republican staff of the Territorial Defence of Serbia, this particular report. So most probably it went to the competent authorities in the ministry or, rather, the General Staff, the intelligence department, and on the basis of this kind of report and similar reports, the most responsible representatives of the Supreme Command at meetings of the Supreme Command would inform us of the different types of problems that exist, and probably of problems like this, too, that they had to confront, which then motivated us to draw attention to this type of deviation and to put an obligation on the command of the sole regular army, that is to say the Yugoslav People's Army, to send those paramilitaries back home, to disarm them and place them under their control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, it's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just brief comment, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. We have in front of us a sheet of paper in B/C/S which is said to be the B/C/S of 948, but I see the difference. Could you clarify the difference between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And first of all, thank you to Your Honour Judge Kwon to remind me that we still have this page that Mr. Kostic provided to us related to the Exhibit 948. Just to explain that they look so different from each other, the English is actually taken from Tanjug, while Mr. Kostic had this -- this page from a collection of documents. But the text is actually absolutely the same. Ms. Dicklich has checked it. What is different is these addressees that are mentioned in the English version are actually in the headline here, mentioned in the headline. There is also a headline given to this document, a name given to the document that does not appear in the English version, and the paragraphs are more dense here in the B/C/S version, but it's exactly the same quotes, except for a difference is also in the English it numbers certain statements as 1 to 4, and in the B/C/S it's only numbered 1 and 2, and the other two paragraphs are not numbered. These are actually the differences. Otherwise, the text is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After number 2 there are two paragraphs in English but there are one paragraph in B/C/S, and I'm not sure whether they are identical. We have to see the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: They are identical but just in a different format.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honours, I actually had intended to put five more documents to Mr. Kostic, if you allow me to do that. It's all related to crime ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, I would put to you now Exhibit 342, tab 11. That's another document from a higher-ranking commander within the JNA, and it's to the command of the 1st Military District, Lieutenant Colonel Milan Jeremija, deputy commander for instructions in matters morale and political propaganda is writing on October 23, 1991. In point 4 of this urgent telegram, he writes: "Activities and occurrences which have a negative impact on the state of morale in the division units." And it says here as the third point under this headline: "In the combat activity zone of the 1st pgmd, the main motive behind the presence of several groups of different paramilitary formations from Serbia, Chetniks, the Dusan Silni detachment, and various self-styled volunteers, is not to combat the enemy but to loot the people's property and engage in sadistic abuse of innocent civilians of Croatian nationality." And he refers then to the village of Lovas. "On one occasion, 80 villagers of Croatian nationality were captured by the TO Lovas and the Dusan Silni detachment; they were then physically abused and four of the Lovas villagers were killed. "After the arrival of the Valjevo Detachment in the village of Lovas, the captured villagers were used for clearing minefields, and 17 villagers were killed. The wounded villagers were refused medical help by the staff of the Sid Medical Centre." This is also a crime base in the Croatian indictment, Mr. Kostic, and do you know about this event when people were taken for clearing minefields in Lovas and got killed by the exercise?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that. This is certainly one of the numerous documents just like the previous two documents, and as we can see, this is sent to the command of the 1st Military District. So the document quite certainly could not have reached me, could not have come into my hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document I would like to put to you is actually an event related to Skabrnja, another crime base.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's not yet an exhibit but perhaps the witness knows about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's the deputy commander of the VPO Major General Mladenic, and it -- it's from the 20th of November, 1991, and related to the Cease-fire Commission. And he says under point 1 the following: "... the Croatian side insisted that one mission team visit Skabrnja and Nadin in the presence of International Committee of the Red Cross representatives. Given as a reason was the fact that the JNA carried out attacks despite the signed cease-fire and that both villages are aflame. A crime against 30 people, who were massacred, (slaughtered), was carried out in Skabrnja." And it continues a lit bit further down: "The mission accepted this request for the reason that the reports are very disturbing and it is necessary to find out the truth and it is in the interests of both sides that the mission as a neutral party does it." And a little bit further down, it says: "With this in mind, the mission requests the JNA to submit to them a detailed written report on the events and the situation in the area." Mr. Kostic, do you know about the European Monitoring Commission complaining about what was happening in Skabrnja and that the JNA then had to provide them with reports? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that. I don't know the purpose of all these documents which are of an operative nature and which go from lower-level units to higher-level units. I really can't say anything about them, nor was I in possession of a document like this at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, you were at that time actually within the Supreme Command of the JNA, and my assumption would simply be that the JNA officials would have informed you, in particular when the UN -- the European observers were complaining on the ground, but you say they didn't. You were not informed.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam, I have told you that at that time all three sides were committing crimes in that civil war.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: That's not an answer --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reports of --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That's not an answer. Now, as you mentioned you visited front lines, I would like to put to you something from the book of Mr. Bulatovic, and it's actually what he writes about your and his visit to the Dubrovnik front on the 13th of October 1991. First of all, do you remember that you visited the front with Mr. Bulatovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The sections I would like you to go to are actually marked, and in the English it's here, named page 7 of 9, but of course it's only three pages that we have here. The first part is that Mr. Bulatovic refers to your visit and the visits on the Herzegovina-Dubrovnik battlefield. We do not need to go into these details, but he is actually explaining what happened while you were there. Mr. Bulatovic is actually describing how you -- your carrier was -- your carrier was actually hit by a long machine-gun burst. Do you remember that, that the carrier in which you and Mr. Bulatovic were travelling were actually shot at? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our vehicle was not hit. There was some shooting, and a member of the JNA was killed, but he was not in our vehicle. He was outside. He was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I heard "carrier" in the interpretation. I'm afraid it was misinterpreted. I was told "your carrier."

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's actually the vehicle in which you were driving. The vehicle.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Driver, not carrier.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And let me just now quote. And this is the middle of page 8, Your Honours. "It was not about a sabotage coup that entered or a lone sniper. A drunken Territorial Defence member from Bar who was in the immediate vicinity shot at us. When he had heard who was in the armoured vehicle, he shouted, 'Now I'm going to kick some ass,' and started shooting with his automatic rifle. Unfortunately, in the chaos that happened, one JNA soldier lost his life. I'm not mentioning his name out of respect. The official version was that he lost his life as a victim of the enemy sniper." Do you recall that, and is it correct what Mr. Bulatovic is writing here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this for the first time when I read Mr. Bulatovic's book. I have to say that this is the first time I came across this in this version. I think it's described incorrectly, just as there are many other incorrect things in his book, as well as fabrications. First of all, our vehicle was not hit at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, your last question.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's one document that I would like to put to Mr. Kostic, and it relates to something that you said on the 6th of February. During your testimony on at that day - it is under 48006 - you answered to a question of His Honour Judge Bonomy, that in the areas where Serbs were a substantial minority and the police station was run by Croats, nothing in that police station would have changed. However, do you know that the police station in Kijevo, that was such a police station that was manned by Croat policemen, was attacked in mid-August 1991 by the JNA and the Martic police?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What precisely happened in Kijevo I can't recall at present, but if this is only about Kijevo, and it's well known what vast number of police stations there were, then it's just the exception that proves the rule. To tell you the truth, I don't know what the ethnic make-up of the population of Kijevo was.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff. I think you must conclude now. Is there something to be tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Just -- I would like to have this Bulatovic book quote marked for identification as the previous one. And, Your Honour, actually the witness has in front of him an exhibit that relates to Kijevo, and it should -- it's Exhibit 463, tab 49. He has it in front of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The witness didn't adopt the exhibits that were put before him by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We have -- I didn't tender anything that was not already an exhibit. I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we have marked for identification some parts of Bulatovic's book. And he's coming, he --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Marked for identification is all right but the application was to have it admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, then I misspoke. But I actually wanted it only to be dealt with like the other parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Marked for identification pending testimony by Mr. Bulatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will form a part of 944.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I've just seen the passage of the transcript. It was my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, the witness still has this one exhibit in front of him and I actually intended to read a little quote from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: It's Kijevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- I think we have been very indulgent.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before Mr. Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Before Mr. Milosevic commences re-examination, if he wishes to re-examine, that is, Mr. Kostic, you had intimated at the beginning of the cross-examination that you had some information in response to a question raised by Judge Bonomy, and I said that I would allow you to provide that information at the end of the cross-examination. You can do that now if you wish, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This refers to the issue of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the provisions from which it may be concluded that one people in Bosnia, or two peoples, can make decisions of a fateful nature to the detriment of the other one or two peoples. I have gone through that constitution and its amendments in detail, and in this connection I would like to say very briefly that in Article 1 on page 98 of the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it is stated, inter alia, that Bosnia and Herzegovina is a state of Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, and of course other peoples. And in another -- in Article 2, or paragraph 2, it is stated that Bosnia and Herzegovina is an integral part of the SFRY. This is all Article 1 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In Article 304, on page 133 of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it says that the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through the republican organs, settles all the relations and matters of an internal nature. In Article 349, which mentions the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in paragraph 11 it says that the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall issue its rules of procedure. This is regulated in the same way in amendment 51, paragraph 9, on page 337, in paragraph 13. In Article 416 on page 149 of the constitution, in the second paragraph it says a change in the constitution shall be adopted -- an amendment shall be adopted if it is voted for by two-thirds of all the delegates in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And just to remind you, Your Honours, the interpreter's correction of the council, there were three councils, or three chambers; the chamber of associated labour, the chamber of municipalities, and the people's chamber. On page 76 in amendment 7, paragraph 2 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you go on, the interpreters have corrected something but it's not clear to me what they've corrected. It was following a reference to voting for something by two-thirds of all the delegates.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Your Honours, not of all the delegates but of all the chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of all the chambers. Thank you. Carry on, Mr. Kostic. It's been clarified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On page 762 in amendment 7, paragraph 2 - that's Official Gazette number 21 in the material we got at the time - it says that the Assembly shall also issue its own rules of procedure. On page 589, in amendment 62, it states that decisions on changes of the territory and the borders shall be made by the Assembly or, rather, there must be a referendum at which all voters decide, and the decision shall be valid if two-thirds of the total number of voters vote in favour. What merits special attention, on page 593, in amendment 78, it is provided that an act on amending the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina can be carried if two-thirds of all the deputies in the Assembly council vote in favour. In amendment 70, paragraph 10 of the constitution, on page 591, it is provided that council will be established to discuss all issues concerning national equality and the equality of all the nations and peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was a constitutional obligation. I believe this amendment was adopted on the 31st of July, 1991. After the multi-party elections, however, at which the Party of Democratic Action won the almost undivided support of the Muslim population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the deputies of this party, in coalition with deputies of the Croatian Democratic Union, rejected the demand to form this council, although this was a constitutional obligation. This council was, therefore, not formed. However, in any case, one can conclude with confidence that not a single decision made by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina and not a single decision made at a referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina was valid or based on the constitution, because without the participation of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there could not be a two-thirds majority in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, nor could there be a two-thirds majority at the referenda. That's 66.6 per cent. That would be a two-thirds majority. And please don't hold me to exact numbers, but I think that the percentage at the referenda was 62 per cent in favour of an independent Bosnia, but the Serbian people boycotted that referendum and did not vote at it. What is of special importance is that there is also a rules of procedure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in those rules of procedure - and this is all in compliance with the constitution - in Article 45 of these rules of procedure, in paragraph 3, it reads follows: "When considering issues relating to the equality of the nations and nationalities, which as such will be established by a new constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency shall decide by consensus." And the last piece of information. On page 137, in paragraph 314 -- in Article 314, paragraph 18, it is said that the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina shall choose and dismiss the member of the Presidency of the SFRY representing Bosnia and Herzegovina. During my testimony, I stated that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic made it impossible for Mr. Bogicevic to continue his work in the Presidency, although he was not authorised to do that by the constitution. It was only the Assembly that could have done that. That's all I had to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, do you know what document the witness has been referring to with the page numbers and --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. I mean, we have -- we provided to the witness, actually, the constitution, and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that's --

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I assume he's quoting from those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that have an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Because we only have it here in the office untranslated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much for the information. These are matters which we'll have to consider, and we'll have the benefit of evidence from constitutional experts. Mr. Milosevic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Kostic, while we're discussing the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which you've just quoted from, and it's the copy that I, too, received from the opposite side over there when you received it, in Article 1 does it say that the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is, et cetera, et cetera, a state of the democratic peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats alike, et cetera? Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says, and I read it out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He read it out. He read it out, Mr. Milosevic, so there's no need to go over that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, in Article 2 it says: "The peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs, Croats, and Muslims." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in Article 3, does it say: "The peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Serbs and Croats and Serbs and Muslims are ensured conditions for the assertion of national values and proportionate representation in the Assemblies of socio-political communities. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's all the 1974 constitution, is it not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't dwell on that any longer. Now, you were provided a moment ago -- well, I can't take this in order, but anyway you were shown a number of documents during the cross-examination. One was a report by the Secretary-General dated the 27th of July, 1992, and it was the one to which you said you had already left your political functions. And do you remember that Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff quoted some passages from that report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Fine. Now, in point 5, she quoted a passage from point 5 where it says the following: "[In English] ... force commander has informed me that all TDF units in Sector East and West have handed over their heavy weapons and that these weapons, which include tanks, artillery, mortars, and anti-aircraft weapons system have been stored in a number of locations." [Interpretation] And she stopped quoting there, whereas the sentence goes on to read as follows. There are no comma, dot, or whatever: [Previous translation continues] "[In English] ... the control of UNPROFOR with a double-lock system." [Interpretation] So the entire quotation contains those elements. Under the control of UNPROFOR, that that's how they were stored, on the double-key system, double-lock system. Is that what you said here and what it says in this report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. And I said that they would be stored under the double-lock system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says here that's what was done. Now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff also quoted something from point 7, the assertion that Vance's plan was being violated. And she says, reading from point 7, that those groups, that border police "[In English] are equipped with automatic rifles and in some cases with machine-guns, in violation of the provisions of the plan which require the police be equipped only with sidearms." [Interpretation] The translation of "sidearms" "bocno oruzje" means in fact pistols. So what does this violation of the plan refer to, the fact that they have rifles and not just pistols? Is that what it says here?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does it also say here that they perhaps used those firearms, that they shot, or was the only violation that they had rifles in addition to the pistols at the border?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the cross-examination, I asked that question. I asked whether any tanks had been abused or misused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, towards the end of point 8, it says, last few sentences: "[In English] However, the Croatian authorities at the highest level as well on the ground have insisted that withdrawal by Croatian army must be contingent on simultaneous withdrawal by the Serb TDF from their positions. Reports from UNPROFOR indicate that while these withdrawals are being generally achieved, the Croatian army is yet to withdraw from Siritovci village in the Drnis area. Efforts are under way by UNPROFOR to effect this withdrawal in order to prevent the further escalation of tension. Moreover, the Croatian authorities have replaced their military in this area with Croatian police which they have so far refused to withdraw, asserting that it is only their army which is required to be withdrawn in accordance with Security Council Resolution 762." [Interpretation] So does it then say there that the Serbs withdrew while the Croatian forces remained or -- and I know --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I know that when we discussed details, according to the Vance Plan, it was provided that the Territorial Defence after the Blue Helmets had taken over, that the Territorial Defence of the Serb Krajina and the Croatian police and other armed units should withdraw. I think that it said to 800 -- to a distance of 800 metres, so as not to jeopardise either side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And just one more point from this document, this report by the UN Secretary-General. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff had quoted some point which in this chapter, which was B, under "Expulsions, Coercion, and Intimidation," under that heading. And she quoted a point listing these incidents, but I'm going to quote another passage from that same chapter and it is point 17. So please listen to what it says in point 17. "[In English] UNPROFOR believes that there is a direct link between this situation -" [Interpretation] that's the situation of pressure, violence, coercion against certain non-Serbs - "[In English] and the presence of large number of refugees in these areas. The influx into the UNPAs of Serb refugees from other parts of Croatia and more recently from Bosnia and Herzegovina continues unabated. The refugees from Croatia, some of whom appear to foresee no possibility --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's a very long passage, so just quote what you need to enable you to ask the question that you wish to put. Don't quote all of it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not going quote the entire paragraph, Mr. Robinson, don't worry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: "[In English] No possibility of return to their homes, especially in western and central Slavonia, have reportedly occupied houses left vacant by the departure of their non-Serb occupants." [Interpretation] Therefore, is what is indicated here the origin of those pressures and conflicts and violence that is taking place in those areas and also the protagonists of that -- those acts of violence?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was a general phenomenon both at that time, before, and later, that where there were conflicts the population always tried to flee to safer areas. And what you just read a moment ago shows that. It indicates the influx, great influx of Serb refugees into those areas which came under the UNPAs zones, the United Nations Protected Areas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You must endeavour not to ask leading questions. Practically every question you have asked so far is a leading question. The question you should have put to the witness just now is, What does this indicate? Instead, you put a question with the answer in it. We have been through this several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'll read out just another portion, and we see what the commander of the forces says, that he is concerned, the UN forces commander, who was General Nambiar at the time. And the last two lines on that page read as follows in 17: "[In English] General Nambiar expressed his serious concern on this issue at meetings with the Belgrade authorities. His interlocutors responded that though they could prevent immigration from Serbia and Montenegro into the UNPAs, they were in no position to do so in the case of refugees from other parts of Croatia whose houses had already been destroyed or those from battle-torn areas of Bosnia-Herzegovina who directly entered neighbouring UNPAs." [Interpretation] What does that tell us, Professor Kostic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, during the cross-examination, I've already answered that question, to all intents and purposes. There were conflicts there. There were clashes there. There was mass migration there, displacement of the population. Everybody sought to go where it was safest, and during the cross-examination, I already said that when the Blue Helmets took up their positions in the area and when the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from the area, we really didn't have any possibility from here of preventing the population from dispersing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just one more question now with respect to that approach and why the UN Secretary-General's report was quoted in the first place. We saw that the arms were handed over according to the double-lock system. Now a very specific question. From the arrival of the Blue Helmets, once they had arrived, was there any attack whatsoever on the part of the forces of the Krajina against Croatian positions?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with certainty that while I occupied the post of vice-president of the Yugoslav state Presidency, until I handed over my duties, I know of not one single incident of that kind or single attack. And later on, on the basis of the information that I received, and just like anybody else I was not in a position to hear of anything like that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kostic, how does that tie in with your inability to recollect anything about the documents which were presented to you indicating anxiety on the part of various people about Serb aggression on the part of paramilitaries or those associated with the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, you seem to be comparing two things here. You're mentioning documents that were shown to me, documents which I'd never seen before, documents which never ever reached me, whereas here in this case we're talking about a document where I was directly involved and in which I invested all my intellectual and physical capabilities to arrive at that peace plan. So I was highly interested and called upon indeed to see whether the peace plan was being respected or not. So you cannot mix and compare those two things. Here I was directly involved and in a certain way responsible for the implementation of that peace plan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Kostic, the question was from the arrival of the Blue Helmets, once they had arrived, was there any attack whatsoever on the part of the forces of the Krajina against Croatian positions? Now, are you claiming universal knowledge from that time on that there were no such attacks? Is that -- you say you were in a position to know that, even though in the past, prior to that, we've seen that there were reports coming through of the involvement of Serb aggression that you don't appear to have been aware of. Now, if you are claiming universal knowledge, what changed after the Blue Helmets arrived to give you that insight into everything that was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy, Mr. Milosevic asked me a specific question. He said from the time the Blue Helmets arrived onwards, were there any attacks by the Territorial Defence against Croatian positions and whether there were any violations of the peace plan. That's how I understood Mr. Milosevic's question. And I said that as far as I knew and during the time that I occupied my post and later on, there were no such attacks. Now, the talks about certain incidents on that territory linked to civilians, to the population, and so on, I think that that's quite another matter altogether and that Mr. Milosevic wasn't asking me about that. He asked me whether there were any violations of the peace plan on the part of the police and other forces on the territory of the Republic of Srpska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you happen to notice that the documents that you were shown here which you had never seen before date back to the times before the UN forces arrived?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning of the cross-examination, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff asked you very briefly something about your information about the population in Krajina at the beginning and at the end and the population in Serbia, and you drew a parallel. Just briefly tell us this, please: What do the changes in population structure indicate if they are compared in Krajina and in Serbia in -- from 1990 to the year 2000?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't have the exact facts and figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about exact figures.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the information I do have at my disposal indicate that in Serbia, on the territory of Serbia, both before the war and after the war, the non-Serb population made up approximately one third of the population, or a little more than one-third of the total population, non-Serbs, of non-Serb ethnicity, and that structure was the same before and after the war. Whereas in Croatia, on the territory of Croatia, the national structure or population structure was so much disturbed that the national structure of Croats, looking at before the war, was increased from 78 to 89 per cent, and the national structure of Serbs was reduced from 12.4 per cent to 4.-something per cent. I don't know the exact digit. In other words, about -- there were about 8 per cent less Serbs in the overall population structure of Croatia afterwards, or today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, Professor Kostic, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff showed you the minutes from a Presidency session of the 13th of August, 1991, and in point 1 there was a quotation there which said that you -- or, rather, the question of the incident was brought up in Dalj, Sarvas, Lovinac in Croatia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO KOSTIC [Resumed]
